title: Endocrine and Reproductive Terminology

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of 'endo-' like the word 'indoors' — it means staying inside. Endocrine glands drop their chemical messengers (hormones) straight inside your body into the blood highway, instead of squirting them out onto a surface. So when you see 'endo,' picture something happening on the inside.

### Question 2

'Glyc/o' means sugar (as in glucose) and '-uria' tells you it is about the urine. Put them together and glycosuria is literally sugar showing up in the pee. The other choices swap in something different — ketones, protein, or just a large amount of urine.

### Question 3

'-rrhea' is the 'flowing' suffix — think of a river running. Diarrhea is stuff flowing out too fast; dysmenorrhea is the monthly flow that comes with pain. Whenever you see '-rrhea,' picture something streaming or flowing.

### Question 4

'Hyper-' is like pressing the gas pedal all the way down — everything goes faster. With hyperthyroidism, the thyroid pours out too much hormone, so the body's engine (metabolism) races: fast heartbeat, sweating, and burning through food. The prefix tells you the whole story before you even learn the details.

### Question 5

The front part 'oophor' just means ovary. The ending changes the meaning: '-ectomy' is like 'exit' — something gets taken out — while '-itis' means 'irritated and inflamed.' Same body part, two very different endings, two very different situations.

### Question 6

The pituitary is like the conductor of an orchestra. It doesn't play every instrument itself, but it signals the other players — the thyroid, adrenal glands, and ovaries or testes — when to start. Because it directs the other glands, we call it the master gland.

### Question 7

Endocrine glands are like sending a text message — it goes invisibly through the blood to wherever it is needed. Exocrine glands are like handing someone a note down a hallway (a duct) to a specific spot, like sweat reaching your skin. 'Endo' means inside the blood, 'exo' means out through a tube.

### Question 8

'Poly-' means 'a lot,' like a polygon has lots of sides. So poly-dipsia is lots of drinking, poly-uria is lots of peeing, and poly-phagia is lots of eating. When someone has all three 'a lots' together, it is a big clue their blood sugar is out of control.

### Question 9

Break the big word into chunks: 'hyster' is the uterus, 'salping' is the fallopian tube, 'oophor' is the ovary, and '-ectomy' means take it out. 'Bilateral' means both sides. So piece by piece, they removed the uterus and both tubes and both ovaries.

### Question 10

'Hypo-' is like a car running low on gas — everything slows down. Low thyroid hormone means the body's engine idles: you feel tired and gain weight. That slowed-down, low-hormone state is hypothyroidism, the opposite of the speeded-up 'hyper' version.

### Question 11

The word already has 'adren' for the adrenal gland — that part is fine. You just need the right ending: '-megaly' means 'big' (think 'mega'). So swap the disease ending for the big ending and you get adrenomegaly, meaning the adrenal gland got enlarged. Watch out for 'aden,' which is a different word part for gland in general.

### Question 12

The ending '-logist' always means 'an expert who studies something,' so the root has to tell you WHAT they study. 'Gynec/o' means woman, so gynec/o + -logist is a gynecologist — the expert in women's reproductive health. The other roots point to males, sex glands in general, or external parts, so they build different terms.
